hamilton.title: Scotland shares England’s debt at Union
hamilton.line: Under the 1707 Union, Scotland took on part of England’s much larger national debt, compensated by a lump sum called the Equivalent.

hamilton.title: Australia’s Commonwealth takes over state debts
hamilton.line: The 1927 Financial Agreement had the federal government take over state debts and created a Loan Council to manage all borrowing.

hamilton.title: Reunified Germany absorbs East German debts
hamilton.line: At reunification, Bonn and the western states borrowed jointly for a unity fund, and federal funds later took over East German debts.

mania.title: The Empire State Building opens mostly empty
mania.line: Built in a late-1920s skyscraper race, the Empire State Building opened 75 percent empty and earned no profit until the 1950s.

mania.title: Spain’s building boom goes bust
mania.line: Spain’s construction boom crashed, leaving empty flats and ghost airports like Ciudad Real, built for €1.1 billion and sold for €10,000.

mania.title: China’s property giant Evergrande defaults
mania.line: China’s long building boom left developers with unsold flats and huge debts, and Evergrande, owing about $300 billion, defaulted.

commune.title: The Women’s March on Versailles
commune.line: Angry at bread prices, Parisians led by market women marched on Versailles and forced the king to leave it for Paris.

commune.title: France’s May 1968 protests and strikes
commune.line: Student protests grew into a general strike of millions that shook de Gaulle’s government, which protesters saw as outdated and repressive.

trusts.title: Parliament ends the East India Company’s monopoly
trusts.line: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company’s monopoly on trade with India, opening it to private British merchants.

trusts.title: The Supreme Court breaks up Standard Oil
trusts.line: Standard Oil once controlled about 90 percent of US refining, and the Supreme Court ordered it split into dozens of firms.

flu.title: The Antonine Plague sweeps Rome’s empire
flu.line: Brought back by soldiers from Mesopotamia, a plague spread along Roman roads and sea lanes, killing perhaps 5 to 10 million.

flu.title: Asiatic cholera reaches Europe and America
flu.line: Cholera from India’s Ganges Delta followed trade routes and armies into Russia and Europe by 1831, then crossed the Atlantic by ship.

flu.title: The 2009 swine flu pandemic
flu.line: A new H1N1 flu found in Mexico spread worldwide within two months, and WHO declared the first flu pandemic in 41 years.

bankrun.title: A run on the Bank of England
bankrun.line: After a French landing in Wales, depositors rushed for gold, and the government let the Bank of England stop paying it out.

bankrun.title: Germany shuts its banks after Danatbank fails
bankrun.line: When Danatbank said it could not pay, panic spread and Germany declared a bank holiday, two years before Roosevelt’s.

bankrun.title: Cyprus shuts banks to stop a run
bankrun.line: To stop a run, Cyprus shut banks for 12 days, capped withdrawals and imposed losses on large deposits in its biggest banks.

einstein.title: The Russell–Einstein Manifesto
einstein.line: Einstein and other leading scientists, with philosopher Bertrand Russell, warned that nuclear weapons could put an end to the human race.

einstein.title: Flu researchers pause risky bird flu work
einstein.line: After two labs made bird flu strains that spread between ferrets, 39 researchers paused such work so its risks could be debated.

sputnik.title: Gagarin becomes the first human in space
sputnik.line: Yuri Gagarin’s orbit beat America into space, and six weeks later Kennedy asked Congress to land a man on the Moon.

sputnik.title: China builds the world’s fastest computer
sputnik.line: China’s Tianhe-1A topped the world supercomputer ranking, and Obama called rivals’ advances “our generation’s Sputnik moment,” urging new research spending.

sputnik.title: China’s reported hypersonic test alarms Washington
sputnik.line: A reported Chinese hypersonic glide vehicle circled the globe, and the top US general called it “very close” to a Sputnik moment.

saigon.title: US Marines leave Beirut
saigon.line: As the Lebanese army it backed collapsed, the US pulled its Marines out of Beirut, months after a bombing killed 241 servicemen.

netscape.title: Gutenberg’s printing press spreads across Europe
netscape.line: After Gutenberg’s Bible of the 1450s, presses spread to over 200 European towns by 1500, turning out millions of books.

netscape.title: Kodak’s $1 Brownie camera
netscape.line: Kodak’s $1 Brownie shipped over 150,000 cameras in its first year, bringing snapshot photography to ordinary people.

netscape.title: Television sweeps into American homes
netscape.line: The share of US homes with a television jumped from 1 percent in 1948 to 75 percent in 1955.

dotcom.title: Britain’s bicycle share bubble bursts
dotcom.line: Hundreds of cycle firms floated as shares soared in 1896, then the index lost over 70 percent and many makers went bust.

dotcom.title: Radio stocks crash with Wall Street
dotcom.line: RCA, the leading radio stock of the 1920s, lost about 98 percent of its value between its 1929 peak and 1932.

dotcom.title: The early-1960s “tronics” boom collapses
dotcom.line: New electronics issues, often named “-tronics”, soared in 1960 and 1961, then many lost 90 percent of their value in 1962.
